findings.title: Rendering an embedded HTML table can exhaust process memory
findings.summary: Rendering a small DOCX containing an HTML altChunk with a large `colspan` allocates one generated grid column per attacker-supplied span value. A single cell with `colspan="1000000000"` causes a billion string writes before layout, bypassing the original package's input-size budgets.

severity.rationale: A document author can deterministically exhaust CPU and memory in a consuming renderer with a tiny input. Availability impact is high for that process, but remote/shared-service deployment is not established and process limits can contain it.

confidence.rationale: Direct source trace establishes attacker-controlled integer parsing and the unbounded allocation loop after admission; no runtime exploit was executed.

taxonomy.category: Uncontrolled resource consumption during HTML expansion

codeEvidence.label: Admission precedes HTML expansion
codeEvidence.explanation: The renderer loads a relationship-targeted chunk from the admitted package and expands it before DOM layout; generated output has no size gate here.

codeEvidence.label: Chunk bytes become HTML and generated WML
codeEvidence.explanation: Attacker-authored HTML is converted locally into a new WML string; archive inflation bounds do not constrain this representation expansion.

codeEvidence.label: HTML colspan accepted without upper bound
codeEvidence.explanation: Any positive span fitting usize survives unchanged; the lower clamp adds no upper bound.

codeEvidence.label: Span values determine generated grid length
codeEvidence.code:
let cols = table
            .rows
            .iter()
            .map(|r| r.iter().map(|c| c.span).sum::<usize>())
            .max()
            .unwrap_or(1)
            .max(1);
        let col_w = 9360 / cols;
codeEvidence.explanation: A one-cell row sets cols directly to the supplied span, independently of input length.

codeEvidence.label: One string write for each column
codeEvidence.explanation: The attacker-sized loop grows the output string by tens of gigabytes for a billion-column cell before later validation could occur.

rootCause.summary: `with_layout()` admits the original DOCX, then `expand()` loads its HTML chunk and passes it to `html_to_wml()`. Cell parsing stores `colspan` as an unrestricted usize. `end_table()` sums the spans into `cols` and emits a grid element for every column, so a short decimal attribute controls huge CPU and allocation work after the input gate.

findings.remediation: Reject spans and total table column counts above a documented limit before construction; use checked addition and enforce a generated-output/work budget shared across all HTML chunks.

counterEvidence: Admission caps compressed/inflated bytes and XML policy before conversion (src/convert/mod.rs:773-778).
SECURITY.md recommends process memory/CPU isolation, which can limit collateral damage.
No shared or remote renderer deployment is established.
limitations: No application code or resource-exhaustion input was executed.
validation.summary: Parent verified the baseline candidate against the actual converter entrypoint and HTML builder. A well-formed one-cell table with a large positive colspan reaches the grid-generation loop with no upper bound; admission limits only the stored input, not this new output.

controls: Original package admission limits do not bound generated table columns.
Host process resource limits mitigate collateral impact.

dataflow.summary: DOCX main-story altChunk relationship -> embedded HTML bytes -> html_to_wml cell span -> row span sum -> repeated grid-column string writes.

impact.rationale: Renderer process CPU and memory exhaustion; a shared host could lose service if its integration provides no isolation.

likelihood.rationale: The numeric span flows directly to the allocation loop and a small input can request billions of iterations.

reachability.summary: A caller-controlled document is sufficient at public conversion APIs; no privileged options or network access are required. The victim must render/layout the supplied document.
preconditions: Victim invokes a rendering/layout API on attacker-authored DOCX.

attackPath.summary: Provide a DOCX whose main story references an embedded HTML table with a huge numeric colspan, then have a victim render it as PDF/PNG or request layout facts.

remediationTests: Assert that a tiny HTML chunk with a huge colspan is refused before grid allocation.
Cover aggregate span overflow, multiple cells/chunks, and valid spans at the inclusive boundary.

originalCandidates.title: Unbounded HTML table colspan expansion causes denial of service
originalCandidates.message: Confirmed strong DoS candidate: src/convert/altchunk.rs parses attacker HTML td/th colspan directly as usize (lines ~564-568), sums spans into cols (lines ~475-481), then emits one w:gridCol per column using for _ in 0..cols (line ~497), no clamp/budget. A tiny embedded HTML altChunk with colspan=1000000000 forces billions of iterations/output despite DOCX admission. Exact call-path/evidence being checked.

findings.title: Rendering embedded CSS multiplies property allocations per selector
findings.summary: A small HTML altChunk stylesheet can exhaust renderer memory before layout. `parse_css()` deep-copies every property value into a separate map for every selector, including unused selectors and unsupported property names; thousands of selectors can retain thousands of copies of one large value.

severity.rationale: Attacker-authored document content can reliably exhaust the consuming process with a modest input. Shared-service deployment is conditional and host process limits reduce collateral impact.

confidence.rationale: Source shows owned String property values, HashMap::clone per selector and retention in Builder with no count or allocation budget.

taxonomy.category: Uncontrolled resource amplification in stylesheet parsing

codeEvidence.label: CSS properties stored as owned strings
codeEvidence.code:
let props: Props = body
            .split(';')
            .filter_map(|d| d.split_once(':'))
            .map(|(k, v)| (k.trim().to_ascii_lowercase(), v.trim().to_string()))
            .collect();
codeEvidence.explanation: A large attacker property value becomes a retained owned String without filtering supported properties or limiting value size.

codeEvidence.label: Deep clone for every selector
codeEvidence.explanation: Distinct comma-separated selectors each retain a deep clone of the complete property map. Allocation is selector count times property bytes.

codeEvidence.label: All styles parsed before body import
codeEvidence.explanation: The parser retains every rule before examining body content, so selectors need not match any element to trigger the allocation.

codeEvidence.label: Admission precedes HTML expansion
codeEvidence.explanation: The renderer loads a relationship-targeted chunk from the admitted package and expands it before DOM layout; generated output has no size gate here.

codeEvidence.label: Chunk bytes become HTML and generated WML
codeEvidence.explanation: Attacker-authored HTML is converted locally into a new WML string; archive inflation bounds do not constrain this representation expansion.

rootCause.summary: After DOCX admission, `expand()` imports an embedded HTML chunk. `html_to_wml()` eagerly calls `parse_css()`, which owns property values as Strings and calls `props.clone()` for every selector. Each distinct selector retains a full copy, making retained memory proportional to selector count multiplied by property size rather than bounded by the original part.

findings.remediation: Share immutable declaration blocks between selectors and enforce aggregate stylesheet work/allocation budgets, selector-count and value-length limits before allocating. Ignore unsupported properties before retention.

counterEvidence: Package input/inflation limits constrain the original HTML but not selector-value multiplication.
Process limits recommended by SECURITY.md can contain the failure.
validation.summary: Parent verified that selector keys are distinct, values are owned Strings, clones remain in Builder, and no maximum or supported-property filter limits the copies. A stylesheet with 10,000 short selectors and one 1 MiB property requests about 10 GiB of retained property bytes from about 1.1 MiB HTML.

dataflow.summary: DOCX chunk -> html_to_wml -> parse_css -> owned property map -> full cloned map retained under each selector.

reachability.summary: Public PDF/PNG/layout conversion loads relationship-targeted HTML after admission. Attacker needs only to supply the document; unused selectors still trigger parsing.

attackPath.summary: Embed a stylesheet containing many distinct comma-separated selectors and a long property value in a DOCX altChunk, then have a victim render the document.

remediationTests: Assert that many selectors sharing a large declaration block remain bounded or are refused before multiplication.
Cover unused selectors, unsupported property names, multiple style blocks, and valid boundary inputs.

originalCandidates.title: Embedded HTML CSS causes multiplicative retained property allocation
originalCandidates.message: parse_css lines 158-166 builds one Props map then deep-clones every property/value for each comma selector. E.g. <style>.s0,...,.s9999{a:<1 MiB value>}</style> is ~1.1 MiB admitted HTML but retains ~10 GiB value clones before any body rendering. html_to_wml lines 607-610 eagerly parses all styles, even unused selectors/properties. Separate CPU/memory multiplier from colspan.

candidate.title: WMF text records read beyond declared record and amplify retained memory
candidate.message: raster_wmf only validates size>=3 and size*2 fits remaining bytes (486-500); EXTTEXTOUT at 623-634 reads y/x/n/options and data.get(at..at+n) against entire file, not current record. Repeating six-byte WMF records [u32 size=3,u16 func=0x0A32] makes each record read next record's func as n=2610 and opts=3 from following size; at=off+22 then copies ~2610 bytes into persistent MetaText despite declared payload zero. ~6 MB body can retain ~2.6 GB text before later layout. Needs nonzero placeable extents and trailing bytes; no runtime reproduction.
